intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that immunodeficiency-35 (IMD35) is caused by homozygous mutation in the TYK2 gene (176941) on chromosome 19p13.2.

checks.claim: Immunodeficiency-35 (IMD35) is caused by homozygous mutation in the TYK2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Here we identified a homozygous Tyk2 mutation in a patient who had been clinically diagnosed with hyper-IgE syndrome.

It says the cytokine signalling defects were restored by putting back an intact TYK2 gene, and that TYK2 deficiency likely accounts for the patient's clinical features. IMD35 is OMIM's name for this disorder, not the paper's.

paragraphs.text: TYK2 deficiency is an autosomal recessive primary immunodeficiency. Kreins et al. (2015) concluded that its core clinical phenotype is mycobacterial and/or viral infection, including disease caused by BCG vaccine and tuberculosis. The first reported patient had been clinically diagnosed with hyper-IgE syndrome (HIES), with atopic dermatitis and elevated serum IgE (Minegishi et al., 2006). Most patients reported later had none of the cardinal features of HIES (Kilic et al., 2012; Kreins et al., 2015).

paragraphs.text: Kilic et al. (2012) reported a Turkish boy, born in 1992, who was the third child of healthy first-cousin parents. He was vaccinated with BCG at 2 months of age. At 8 months, left axillary lymphadenopathy was detected, and he went on to develop disseminated BCG infection with generalized fistulous lymphadenopathy and fever. He later had neurobrucellosis, a generalized tonic-clonic seizure, severe sensorineural hearing loss, severe cognitive impairment, lacunar infarcts on MRI, pneumonia, and herpes zoster of the maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve. Serum IgE concentrations measured at ages 2, 11, 16, and 18 years were normal or slightly high (80, 115, 218, and 155 IU/ml, respectively). His PPD skin test was negative and his antibody response to tetanus toxoid was low. He had no atopy or eczema, staphylococcal skin infections, skeletal or dental abnormalities, or candidiasis, and his serum IgG, IgM, and IgA were normal. Kilic et al. (2012) noted that, unlike the first Japanese patient with TYK2 deficiency, their patient had none of the cardinal features of HIES. They suggested that TYK2 deficiency be considered in patients with BCG disease, particularly when accompanied by severe herpesvirus infections, even without features of HIES.

paragraphs.text: Kreins et al. (2015) restudied the Japanese patient (P1) originally reported by Minegishi et al. (2006). He was born to consanguineous parents, had atopic dermatitis from 1 month of age, and had recurrent bacterial and viral infections from 1 year of age. His infections included recurrent Staphylococcus aureus skin abscesses, BCGitis, nontyphi Salmonella enterocolitis with sepsis, parainfluenza virus 3 pneumonia, recurrent oral herpes simplex virus infections, molluscum contagiosum, mild oral candidiasis, pneumonia without pneumatocele, otitis, and sinusitis. He also had ocular sarcoidosis. Repeated immunologic studies showed hypereosinophilia (701-800/microliter) and high serum IgE concentrations (1,430-2,100 IU/ml). He was 30 years old at the time of the report.

paragraphs.text: In kindred C, which was Moroccan and consanguineous, the girl P3 was hospitalized at 13 years of age with suspected abdominal tuberculosis. Despite antimycobacterial treatment her abdominal complaints persisted, and she developed ascites and a psoas abscess within a few months. Treatment was restarted, but she was readmitted with bacterial meningitis and died 15 months after symptom onset. Her younger brother, P4, was hospitalized at 8 months of age for meningitis of unknown etiology. He also had recurrent otitis, urinary tract infections, asthma, eczema of the ear canal, and high eosinophil levels, but not high serum IgE. At age 15 years he was receiving no treatment (Kreins et al., 2015).

paragraphs.text: In an international cohort of children hospitalized for COVID-19 pneumonia, Zhang et al. (2022) identified 3 unrelated TYK2-deficient children (P2, P3, and P4), aged 2, 4, and 9 years, each born to a different set of consanguineous Turkish parents. P2, a girl, was hospitalized for moderate COVID-19 pneumonia but did not need oxygen therapy. She had been hospitalized for sepsis as a neonate, was admitted to the ICU twice for fever and dyspnea before 5 months of age, was diagnosed with Kawasaki disease at 11 months, and was hospitalized at 2 years for infection with the varicella-zoster virus (VZV) vaccine. P3 and P4, both boys, were admitted to the ICU for critical COVID-19 pneumonia requiring high-flow oxygen therapy. P3 had been hospitalized for neonatal sepsis and was admitted to the ICU for influenza pneumonia at 3 years. P4 had recurrent bronchitis requiring hospital admission and inhaler therapy. Neither boy had an adverse reaction to MMR vaccination. The 3-year-old younger sister of P3, who had the same genotype, had a history of critical influenza pneumonia requiring intubation and ventilation and of disseminated varicella, but had not been infected with SARS-CoV-2 and remained seronegative. The authors found critical COVID-19 pneumonia in unrelated TYK2-deficient patients surprising, because TYK2 deficiency impairs but does not abolish cellular responses to type I IFNs. They noted that more infected TYK2-deficient patients were needed to estimate penetrance, which may be incomplete.

paragraphs.text: In 3 unrelated Turkish children (P2, P3, and P4) born to consanguineous parents and hospitalized for moderate or critical COVID-19 pneumonia, Zhang et al. (2022) identified homozygosity for a frameshift variant in the TYK2 gene (P216Rfs*14). The variant had previously been shown to cause loss of expression, and the authors confirmed that it was loss of function. The younger sister of P3, who had critical influenza pneumonia and disseminated varicella, carried the same genotype. Autosomal recessive inheritance was confirmed by family segregation analysis. Patient fibroblasts failed to control SARS-CoV-2 replication and to respond to IFN-alpha-2b.
